The fundamental basis of capitalism is producing a good or service for x and then selling it for x+y where y is profit, and the entire goal of the system is to maximize y to no end. The thing that's supposed to balance the inherent greed of capitalism is competition. But this doesn't always work. Socialism is not the opposite of capitalism. On Voat when most people talk about socialism, they mean and/or conflate it with communism.

Communism is the system where all production is evenly split up and merit is meaningless. Socialism, by contrast, works hand in hand with capitalism. The big difference in socialism is that industries where the capitalist system can not effectively work are state run. So for instance in the United States fire departments are already socialized. The reason this is good is because critical industries don't really work well in a capitalist system. Imagine your house is on fire and I'm the first fire fighter that gets there. Like a good capitalist, I ask so how much are you willing to pay me to save your house? The answer is obviously completely out of touch with the realities of my cost and so I can charge arbitrarily large amounts.

So for instance an industry that nearly all of the developed world has socialized is healthcare. It's again the same problem. You're very ill and I'm a doctor who can treat you. How much are you willing to pay me? The answer is completely out of touch with my costs. This is why millions of Americans have over time ended up losing everything they had and having to declare bankruptcy just because they came down with an unexpected sickness.

Along with this, socialism also tends to have a better 'safety net'. The whole idea of socialism is to provide a better living experience for as many people as possible while still allowing merit to allow those of capability to flourish with no limits. It's not as easy as in the United States to go from rich to super rich to ultra rich since you'll pay more in taxes and there will be less subsidies and other forms of corporate welfare and handouts, but it's far easier than in the United States to go from middle class to upper class, and even easier still to go from poor to middle class. This is why if you look at socioeconomic mobility, or the rate of movement from one socioeconomic class to another, the United States is one of the lowest in the world. And the countries we label as "socialist", Scandinavia in particular, have the highest socioeconomic mobility in the world.

The nice thing is that what I'm saying isn't hypothetical. Costs aren't even close so there's no real debate there. Here are the OECD data on healthcare costs. You probably want to swap it into per capita, purchasing parity, but we spend more per capita than any other country on the planet by a very wide margin.

Here are the OECD data for healthcare outcomes. On the left side click on "Health Care Quality Indicators" and you can see a variety of fields and how people fare on average. For instance you can see cancer care survival rates, or how often foreign bodies are inadvertently left inside of patients after surgery. The United States healthcare outcomes are far from extraordinary. We tend to be run of the mill. And our defensive doctors aren't exactly defensive. Defensive medicine isn't defensive in terms of defending against leaving something in someone during surgery.

It means running tests that the doctor may not feel are appropriate or warranted but are done specifically to form a defense against potential future lawsuits. These are paid for by the insurance company, so you don't know the difference but the costs percolates through the system in all sorts of ways.
